utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: The witness can make the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you. Please sit down. Yes, the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Examined by Ms. Reidy:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, ma'am. Can I ask you first to please state your full name for the record.

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC
utterances.text: Of course. My name is Snjezana Delic, maiden name Mandelic [phoen]. I was born on the 31st of July, 1955, in Osijek. I was born in Osijek, but I spent all of my child-hood, and I went to pre-school -- elementary school and secondary school in Samac. After completing secondary school, I went to Sarajevo to the faculty of economy -- economics. And then I went back to Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And could you just clarify for us in the courtroom. Osijek, where exactly is Osijek located?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC
utterances.text: Osijek is in the Republic of Croatia, before Croatia was a constituent republic of the socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. But it is still in the Republic of Croatia, of what is today the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. So I -- you were born in Osijek, but you grew up in Bosanski Samac. Did you marry in Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC
utterances.text: Yes. I met my current husband, Dragan Delic, in Bosanski Samac, and we have been married since 1979.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you have any children?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC
utterances.text: Yes. I have two children: a daughter, born in 1981; and a son, born in 1984, Almira and Fedja.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. So you told us that you went back to Samac after you'd studied economics in Sarajevo. And did you then begin working back in Samac? And if so, could you tell us where you began working.

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC
utterances.text: Precisely. After graduating, after getting my diploma, I found out there was a vacancy for a professor of economics in the primary school -- at the secondary school of Bosanski Samac, which I also attended myself. So I started to work there as -- at that school as a professor of economics.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And did you continue to work at that school in Bosanski Samac until April 1992?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. I worked continuously in that school until April; the 16th of April, to be precise, 1992, until practically 7.00 in the evening. It all ended with a teachers' meeting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you were working and living with your family in Bosanski Samac in April 1992; that's correct, is it?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The technical school, or the secondary school where you were teaching, could you tell me whether it was -- there was an ethnic mix, both of students and both of your colleagues and the working staff?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC
utterances.text: There certainly was. We made no discrimination at all. Among the teaching staff, all ethnic groups and convictions were represented, and we didn't notice any difference ourselves. We socialised and communicated normally.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And could I ask you, what -- if you are -- if you are to identify yourself with any national group, how would you identify yourself?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC
utterances.text: As my parents are Croat, I also declare myself as a Croat but from Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Can I ask you about some people -- if you knew some people at the time that you were living in Bosanski Samac. And the first person I'd ask you about was whether you ever knew somebody called Miroslav Tadic in 1992 in Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC
utterances.text: I did know Mr. Tadic, also from school and generally from about the town, because that's where he also lived with his family.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know whether Mr. Tadic had a nickname?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC
utterances.text: Miroslav Tadic, nickname Brko, which means moustache.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Could I just ask you, the Miroslav Tadic you've been talking about, could you see if he's in this room today, and if so, could you just indicate for us where he is.

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC
utterances.text: He is sitting second -- in the second seat from where I'm looking, behind.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Can I just seek clarification, because for the record, that's not going to be clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: No, it's not clear.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said, "He's sitting second, in the second seat where I'm looking." Those directions are not exactly clear for me. Could you be more precise to where this man is sitting. If pointing would be of assistance, then perhaps we can describe where you're pointing on the record.

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC
utterances.text: He is sitting in the second chair, and he still has a moustache.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the second chair on which row in this courtroom?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC
utterances.text: To my left-hand side. He's to my left, in that room. I don't know how to explain.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would it be fair to say that behind the row you're talking about, there's a large window? Is that the row you're talking about, the row underneath the window?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC
utterances.text: Precisely. Precisely. That's what I meant. I'm sorry I was so inaccurate in my directions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's not a problem. It's just for the record. I'd like to ask you about a second person, somebody called Simo Zaric. Did you know someone called Simo Zaric in Bosanski Samac in 1992?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC
utterances.text: I did. I knew him too, because he lived and worked in Bosanski Samac, so I know him from around town. But I also know the family of his wife, and I know him by his son, who attended the school where I worked as a teacher.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And again, for the record, if you see him here today, could you just let us know where he is located.

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC
utterances.text: Well, following the same logic, he's sitting to my left-hand side, in the first seat beneath the glass window.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can I then ask you about another person who -- if you knew this person in Bosanski Samac in 1992, anybody called Dr. Blagoje Simic.

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC
utterances.text: No, not personally.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you know -- do you know if there was somebody in Bosanski Samac in 1992 called Mr. Blagoje Simic, or Dr. Blagoje Simic, although you didn't know him personally?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC
utterances.text: I knew of him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Again, you say you didn't know him personally, but would you recognise him if he was -- if you were to see him in the courtroom today?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure. I rather wouldn't answer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And then there's a third person -- sorry, a fourth person, a Mr. Milan Simic. Did you know Mr. Milan Simic?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC
utterances.text: I knew Milan Simic as a student of my school. I was his teacher for one year, one term, but we didn't come across each other after that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Could the record reflect that the first two defendants, Mr. Miroslav Tadic and Mr. Simo Zaric, were identified by the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mrs. Delic, I'd just like to ask you about the time period March and the first half of April 1992. And I'd like just to ask whether when you were working in the school, if you noticed any changes or events that indicated to you a rise in the ethnic tensions within the municipality of Bosanski Samac at that time.

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC
utterances.text: Certainly. The very fact that the war in Croatia was already underway, we had to feel tensions in our town, in our school, and the very fact that national parties had been established and took up seats in the parliament in 1990, and it was further aggravated by the fact that in 1992, tensions and -- began to rise among ethnic groups, and people started to differentiate and to declare themselves as one or the other ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you at this stage decide to join any of the national parties that had been established?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC
utterances.text: I was not a member of any party at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was your husband or any of your immediate family a member of any of the national parties at the time?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC
utterances.text: My husband was not a member of any political party either. We were a mixed marriage, a marriage of mixed ethnicity. And we believed that being who we are, we could not subscribe to any of these parties.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And specifically in the school, did you notice any changes or incidents which reflected this change of ethnic tension that you've just described?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC
utterances.text: In the school itself, tension was felt in the very fact that many students missed classes. Students and parents explained this by saying that in the surrounding villages from which these students came from, the situation was unsafe and tense. This was certainly also felt in the work of the school and in the teaching.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Have you -- did you ever hear at the time of a group called the 4th Detachment?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC
utterances.text: I heard that such a group or such detachment had been established and that they were even armed, or rather, that members of that unit or detachment possessed weapons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you yourself hear of or know of any individuals who were members of that 4th Detachment?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC
utterances.text: I did. But it's difficult to name all these people now. But I can give you an example where it is obvious. One of my colleagues, Nada, told me that her brother-in-law had come back from somewhere one evening and took out a rifle -- an automatic rifle from his car and that he belonged to such a movement. Her brother-in-law's name was Dzuheric, nicknamed Coc.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And can I clarify -- did your colleague say that her brother-in-law had come back -- come home with a weapon and explain that he belonged to the 4th Detachment, or was it some other movement?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC
utterances.text: She saw him coming into the house, standing on the balcony, and she saw him take out that rifle from the car, and she knew that he was a member of that movement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you say "that movement," are you speaking about the 4th Detachment?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC
utterances.text: Yes, about the 4th Detachment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You testified that you worked as a teacher up until about 7.00 p.m. on the 16th of April, 1992. After you finished your teachers' meeting, what did you do then?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC
utterances.text: After that, I went back home and stayed there together with my husband and two children.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I understand from your testimony that you didn't go to work on the 17th of April. Could you explain what happened between the 16th and 17th of April that made you decide that you shouldn't be going to work on the 17th.

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC
utterances.text: In the night, from the 16th/the 17th of April, 1992, about 3.00 a.m., there was an explosion. I'm not an expert in weapons or detonations, but it was not shooting. It was an explosion. After all the tension and constant rumours that something was about to happen and that peace could not go on in any case, I realised that some sort of conflict is underway somewhere in the town or at the entrance into the town and that something had begun. I didn't know whether it was an attack or a conflict.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And then on the 17th of April, I take it you stayed at home?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC
utterances.text: Of course. That morning, we stayed indoors. And early in the morning, I saw next to my house in the street where we resided, I saw armoured vehicles passing by, escorted by men in camouflage uniforms, and that something out of the ordinary is taking place in the street, that nobody is coming out of their houses and that nothing resembles a normal working day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Where in Bosanski Samac is your house located? Right in the centre, or is there any other landmark nearby your house?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC
utterances.text: The house was in the Bulevar Valucia [phoen], that is, the street that goes from the Zelnici [phoen] stadium to the cultural centre. In any case, it's not central in the strict sense of the word.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, these men that you saw walking by in camouflage uniform, did you recognise or know any of those men who were accompanying the armoured vehicles?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC
utterances.text: I did not recognise these men. I had the impression that they had come from outside, and I had never seen such vehicles around town before. What transpired in the next few moments was that an announcement was made through a megaphone, or some sort of loudspeaker system, to the effect that all men should come out of their houses and bring out any weapons they may have.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did your husband obey that instruction from the megaphone?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC
utterances.text: He did, and the other neighbours were outside as well, mainly those who were not of Serb nationality. We noticed, actually, that all our Serb neighbours were wearing drab olive uniforms that day and carrying weapons. The people who issued the orders to surrender and collect the weapons spoke in the Ekavian dialect, which told us that they came from Serbia. At any rate, they were not from Bosnia or from the local parts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And did your husband have any weapons to surrender?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You mentioned a man earlier in your testimony whose nickname was Coc and I believe whose name was Dzuheric. Did you see him at all during this first day?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC
utterances.text: He showed up the next day, accompanying a truck with people wearing military uniforms, and they were about to collect any remaining weapons. He was the one who knew the locals who lived on that street, and he showed who lived where.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And you said, "The people wearing military uniforms." Are these the people who you believed to have come from Serbia, or were they other local people in military uniform?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC
utterances.text: Locals of Serb ethnicity were all wearing drab olive uniforms that morning. It looked as if they had been mobilised as soldiers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the people who were wearing military uniforms on the truck with this person nicknamed Coc, were they locals in military uniform, or were they these people from Serbia in military uniform that you spoke about seeing on the first day?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC
utterances.text: I didn't know them. I don't know about them, because I didn't hear them speak. All I know is that they were in military uniform.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you didn't recognise them?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, during these first few days after the 17th of April, did you stay at home, or did you try to leave your house? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC
utterances.text: The first three days, we did not leave our house. My husband, my children, and myself, we stayed indoors and tried to make do with the food we had inside. Then the third day, I noticed that it was pretty quiet 4 and neighbours were moving about. I noticed that some of our neighbours, who were not muslim, were moving through the street wearing white bands and were going somewhere in the direction of the town. I thought to myself that I could go out, too, and visit my mother, who lived on the same street, see how she was doing. And indeed, I did so. On my way to her place, to the residential building where she lived, I noticed that the primary school had burnt down halfway.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And in these first four days, your visit to your mother was the only time that you ventured outside of your house; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC
utterances.text: The first three days, that was the only time I ventured outside, indeed. And after that, I stayed indoors for another two days.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. When you were indoors, did you receive any information or instructions from the authorities about what was going on or changes that had taken place, restrictions that had been imposed?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC
utterances.text: We got our first piece of information on the first or perhaps the second day through the local radio, Radio Samac, which announced itself as the Serbian radio of Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what sort of information did this Serbian radio of Samac give you?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC
utterances.text: At first, the announcements began by saying that Samac had been liberated and that a curfew had been introduced, together with a restriction of movement, that is, a ban on movement, from 9.00 p.m. to 6.00 a.m.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the announcements on the radio ever say who was in charge or say who was making the announcement, who was responsible for this information?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC
utterances.text: As responsible for information, it was mostly the Crisis Staff that was mentioned, the Crisis Staff of the Serbian Municipality of Bosanski Samac, or as the Serbian municipality of the Serb people of Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So do I take it that, for example, when you were told that a curfew had been introduced, the announcement indicated that it was being introduced by the authority of the Crisis Staff, or the Serbian municipality of the Serb people?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC
utterances.text: That's how I understood such information, yes. And it was clear to me that the administration of the town was taken over by one ethnic group which stated that it was the Serbian municipality with Serbian people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that you stayed at home in a total, I think, for five -- five days. Can you please tell us what happened on the fifth day of the takeover.

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC
utterances.text: On the fifth day, in the morning, I tried to get us some supplies, some food. However, the square where the bread shop was and shop for other food, it wasn't possible to buy anything. But the Serbian Red Cross was distributing bread and milk there. So I received some of those products as well there that morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And were you -- was your husband at any stage arrested?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC
utterances.text: At that time, he was still at home, until the afternoon of that same day. That was the 22nd of April, 1992. We heard the phone ring. I answered the phone. I didn't recognise the voice at the other end, but they said that they were looking for their friend. So I handed over the receiver. After the conversation, he said that he had been called to the police station, that Stevan Todorovic had called him to the police station for some information or talks about the company, and that he had to leave right away.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And could you just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Ms. Reidy. The witness mentioned, page 69, lines 15 and 16, that it was the Serbian Red Cross that was distributing bread and milk. So are we talking about Serbian from Serbia Red Cross? I mean, I'd just like to know where this particular Red Cross group was coming from precisely.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mrs. Delic, can I ask you to go back to your explanation of how you received some bread and milk. You spoke about the Serbian Red Cross. Can you explain to us what you mean by the "Serbian Red Cross."

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC
utterances.text: I think that it was the Red Cross that was organised by the new authorities, the so-called authorities of the Serb Municipality of Bosanski Samac, as they called it. And it was comprised of local citizens.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know of its existence before the 17th of April? Was there always a local Serbian Red Cross, or is this a new institution, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC
utterances.text: The fact that it called itself "Serbian," was something new. Up until that time, nothing was named "Serbian," such as the Red Cross or anything like that. There was a Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So there was a local Red Cross before the 17th of April, 1992?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then how did you learn that it was called the "Serbian Red Cross"? Was this information the people selling the bread gave you, or did you learn it from another source?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC
utterances.text: I got this information from people who were distributing the food, that it was the newly formed Serbian Red Cross, and that they were going to help us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I think you said the people who were working for the Serbian Red Cross, they were locals and not people from Serbia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC
utterances.text: Yes, they were locals. People who didn't do that kind of work before, but in these new emergency conditions, they took upon themselves the duties of helping or being members in a Serbian Red Cross organisation like that. They were wearing military uniforms also.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Is that of assistance to Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes, thanks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Again, it's another question to clarify some of your testimony. You had also told us that a phone call had come to your house and that you had passed the receiver to your husband, and that he told you Stevan Todorovic wanted him to come to the police station to talk about the company. Could you just explain to me what -- when you say "the company," what company you're talking about.

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC
utterances.text: Yes. It's true that he said that. When I say "company," I'm thinking of the Mebos work organisation that my husband worked at as a manager.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And what exactly was the Mebos? Was it a manufacturing factory? What sort of company was it?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC
utterances.text: It was a work organisation within a larger work organisation called Energoinvest which had its headquarters in Sarajevo. But in Bosanski Samac, that factory was manufacturing water heaters, barrels. So they were making metal industrial products, in any case.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. So did your husband in fact then leave to go to the police station?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC
utterances.text: He went to the police station. And after about an hour or two, he called on the telephone and only said that, "I have this opportunity. I have been permitted to call you, and I will be staying here for a while." After that, he didn't come home.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he able to say why he would be staying there for a while?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC
utterances.text: No, he didn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So your husband never came home. And did your husband ever come home again before you left Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC
utterances.text: No. He was never permitted to leave the premises where he was detained.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were you at any stage given any information from any official from the Serbian Municipality of Bosanski Samac as to the fact that your husband was detained or why he was detained, or any information about him?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC
utterances.text: I never received an official explanation, any kind of information of that sort. I sought through questioning, by questioning people of Serb ethnicity whom I believed could provide such information to me. They were in managerial functions or had some kind of connection with the Crisis Staff or the leadership of the new Serbian authorities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But nobody gave you any official explanation as to the reason for your husband's arrest?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So after the 22nd of April, I take it you were left alone with your two children in your house.

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to just ask you about what happened to you and your children between that date, the 22nd of April, and when you came to leave Bosanski Samac. Did you continue to have electricity all the time between April and when you left Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC
utterances.text: No. In any case, life was less and less normal. It was impossible to lead any kind of normal life. First of all, because officially I no longer performed my work duties, so nobody informed me that I had been fired from my job. But in any case, I was never included in any kind of official schedules or duties. I had to live on what I owned up until then, on the things that I happened to have at that time. For me, it was particularly difficult when I went at one time during those days to the bank, where they still had records of our checking accounts, where we did have some money, when I was told that I didn't have any right to take out any money because my husband was in prison and that I had to have permission from the Crisis Staff in order to withdraw money.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. So can I just clarify that testimony, and then I'd like to go back and cover some more points. But you were told in the bank that you had to get permission from the Crisis Staff to have access to your husband's account; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Maybe for the record I'd just ask one more question, and then it's almost 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. And I also wanted clarification. Was it just her husband's account? Was she -- it was one account that they had. She didn't have her own.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Or was it a joint account?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mrs. Delic, could you just clarify that. Was it your husband's account? Was it a joint account? Did you have your own account?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC
utterances.text: I had my own account, because I worked up until that time. And my husband had his own separate account, but I was authorised to make withdrawals from his account and he was authorised to make withdrawals from my account. But at that moment, I could not take money out from his account, because in cases -- for example, because he was in prison, this was not possible to do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Was it possible to withdraw money from your own account?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: All right. You can proceed, Ms. Reidy.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When we continue tomorrow, I'm going to ask you more questions about your time. But just for the record, could you tell me when you left Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC
utterances.text: I left Bosanski Samac on the 4th of September, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: I think that will be the last question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SINGH
utterances.text: Just one question as a follow-up from the Court. Any reason why you could not withdraw from your own account?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I wasn't given any explanation. I connected this to the fact that my husband was in prison, and that as a family, we were being punished.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SINGH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: All right. We shall adjourn until tomorrow afternoon at 14.15 hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: at 6.01 p.m., to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 27th day of February, 2002, at 2.15 p.m. 23 24 25
